property_summary: After scheduling and executing an operation, calling supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) returns true on reference but false on buggy contract.
Call supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) after deploy; reference returns true, mutant returns false.
After scheduling and executing a valid operation via executeBatch, call supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) returns true on reference but false on buggy contract.

After scheduling and executing a valid operation (cancel should succeed on reference but fails on mutant due to missing admin role check in supportsInterface), test that c.getTimestamp(id) returns _DONE_TIMESTAMP (1) on reference but not on mutant.

After deploying C with proposer and executor roles set to this contract, scheduling an operation with a delay of 1800 seconds and waiting for it to be ready, calling cancel on the operation's id reverts on the reference (because caller lacks TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE) but succeeds on the mutant (which incorrectly returns false for supportsInterface(EXECUTOR_ROLE) and thus allows the executor to cancel).
A call to supportsInterface(IAccessControl.interfaceId) returns true on the reference but false on the mutant.
Reference returns true for supportsInterface(IAccessControl.interfaceId) while the mutant returns false.

After deploying C and scheduling a batch, the reference contract's supportsInterface(IAccessControl.interfaceId) returns true while the mutant returns false, and this divergence is observed via a public read.
After deploying C with proposers and executors as empty arrays, calling supportsInterface(IAccessControl.interfaceId) on the reference returns true, while on the mutant it returns false.
After deploying C, calling supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) on the reference returns true, while on the mutant it returns false.

If `supportsInterface` is called after deployment, the reference returns true for both IAccessControl and ERC165 interface IDs, but the buggy version returns false for the ERC165 interface ID, causing the assertion `c.supportsInterface(0x01ffc9a7)` to diverge.
The scenario calls supportsInterface(0x01ffc9a7) after deployment; the reference returns true (ERC165 support), the buggy version returns false, causing the assertion to fail on the buggy version.
After deployment, calling supportsInterface for the ERC165 interface ID (0x01ffc9a7) returns true on the reference but false on the buggy version.
After deploying the contract, the reference returns true for supportsInterface(0x01ffc9a7) (the ERC165 interface ID), but the buggy version returns false.
When calling supportsInterface with the exact interface ID of IERC165, the reference contract returns true while the buggy contract returns false.
Call supportsInterface with the interface ID of IERC165 after the contract is deployed; the reference returns true, the buggy returns false.
Call supportsInterface with IERC165's interface ID; the reference returns true, the buggy (AND) returns false.
Call supportsInterface with IERC165's interface ID on the deployed C; reference returns true, buggy (AND) returns false.
After deploying C with proposers=[address(this)] and executors=[address(this)], calling supportsInterface with IERC165's interface ID returns true on the reference (OR) and false on the buggy (AND).

After granting PROPOSER_ROLE to a user, that user schedules an operation, then cancels it. In the reference, cancel succeeds because hasRole correctly returns true; in the mutant, hasRole returns false causing cancel to revert.

Grant EXECUTOR_ROLE to address(0) (open role). In reference, execute reverts because hasRole(EXECUTOR_ROLE, address(0)) returns false, so the open-role check fails and _checkRole reverts. In mutant, hasRole returns true, so onlyRoleOrOpenRole allows execution to proceed, causing a divergent revert.
Grant PROPOSER_ROLE to an account, schedule an operation, then have that account cancel it. In the reference, cancel succeeds; in the mutant, cancel reverts because hasRole returns inverted.

After granting PROPOSER_ROLE to the contract itself, the contract schedules an operation. Then a non-PROPOSER (address(this)) tries to cancel; in the reference, hasRole returns false and cancel reverts, while in the mutant, hasRole returns true and cancel succeeds.

After setting EXECUTOR_ROLE's admin to itself and revoking TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE from address(this), calling execute (which triggers _afterCall) reverts in the reference because hasRole(TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE, address(this)) returns false, but in the mutant it succeeds because the inversion makes it return true, causing a divergent revert vs. success.

In the reference, getRoleAdmin(PROPOSER_ROLE) returns the admin role TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE; in the bug, it returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00). This causes cancel(bytes32) to revert in the reference (caller lacks TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE to complete _afterCall) but succeed in the bug.

Deploy with proposers=[address(this)] and executors=[]: in reference getRoleAdmin(PROPOSER_ROLE) returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00), so cancel(id) reverts in _afterCall because caller lacks admin role; in bug getRoleAdmin(PROPOSER_ROLE) returns 0x00, so cancel succeeds without admin check.

BUG: In reference, cancel after scheduling and before executors set reverts because _afterCall does not have TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE; in bug, getRoleAdmin(PROPOSER_ROLE) returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00) so cancel succeeds despite missing admin role in _afterCall.

Calling cancel(bytes32) after scheduling an operation: in the reference, _afterCall reverts because msg.sender lacks TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE, but in the bug, getRoleAdmin(PROPOSER_ROLE) returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00), so cancel succeeds.

When getRoleAdmin(PROPOSER_ROLE) is called, the reference returns TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE while the bug returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00), causing the _afterCall in cancel(bytes32) to revert in the reference but succeed in the bug.

When operation id has timestamp = 0 (never scheduled), P.isOperation(id) returns false (since 0 > 0 is false) but M.isOperation(id) returns true (since 0 >= 0 is true), which affects cancel: P reverts because isOperationPending (which calls isOperation) returns false, but M proceeds because isOperationPending returns true (since getTimestamp > _DONE_TIMESTAMP? Actually 0 > 1 is false, so isOperationPending also returns false? Wait, re-evaluating: isOperationPending returns getTimestamp(id) > _DONE_TIMESTAMP = 1, so 0 > 1 is false. However the mutant changes isOperation only. In cancel, require(isOperationPending(id)) checks that. For id with timestamp=0, both P and M have isOperationPending return false (since 0 > 1 false). So cancel reverts in both. To trigger a divergence we need a timestamp > 0 but <= _DONE_TIMESTAMP? _DONE_TIMESTAMP=1, so the only integer between 0 exclusive and 1 inclusive is 1? Actually >0 and <=1 means timestamp=1. Then isOperation returns true for both (>=0 and >0 both true for 1). isOperationPending returns 1 > 1 = false. So cancel reverts both. Or timestamp=2: isOperation P: 2>0 true, M: 2>=0 true; isOperationPending: 2>1 true. Then cancel works for both. So the only boundary where they differ is timestamp exactly 0. But then cancel reverts both because isOperationPending(0) = 0>1 = false. So cancel cannot be the entry that distinguishes them. The statement says 'Driven through the public/external entry cancel(bytes32), P and M differ in this way: a call isOperation(args) that completes (does not revert) in both P and M, but returns different values: the return value of P.isOperation(args) differs from that of M.isOperation(args).' Wait, it says the call isOperation(args) differs, not cancel. So the test can simply call isOperation directly. For id with no timestamp (default 0), P.isOperation returns false (0>0 false), M.isOperation returns true (0>=0 true). So we can assert that. The test: setIdle, call c.isOperation(someId) and assert false for P, true for M. That's a direct divergence. The test must end with assertTrue reading c's behavior. So call c.isOperation(someId) and compare to expected. That works.
isOperation returns false for an unscheduled operation (timestamp 0) in P, but true in M due to '>= 0' condition.
For an unscheduled operation (timestamp = 0), c.isOperation(someId) returns false in the reference (0 > 0 is false) but true in the mutant (0 >= 0 is true).
For an unscheduled operation (timestamp = 0), calling isOperation(id) returns false in the reference but true in the mutant.
For an operation id that has never been scheduled (timestamp is 0), P's isOperation(id) returns false (0 > 0 is false) while M's returns true (0 >= 0 is true).

After scheduling an operation, calling cancel with a valid id should succeed on the reference but revert on the buggy contract because isOperation returns false (0==0) causing the pending check to fail.

After scheduling an operation and then warping past its delay, calling isOperationPending returns true on reference but false on buggy because isOperation returns !=0 vs ==0, causing cancel to succeed on reference and revert on buggy.

After scheduling an operation, cancel with an invalid id (that has never been scheduled) returns false for isOperationPending on the reference but true on the buggy contract, causing cancel to succeed on the buggy contract (incorrectly deleting the timestamp) while reverting on the reference.

After scheduling an operation and canceling it, calling isOperation with the operation's id returns false on the reference (since timestamp becomes _DONE_TIMESTAMP=1, which is >0) but true on the buggy contract (since 1 == 0 is false).

After calling cancel with an id of a previously scheduled operation, P keeps the timestamp at _DONE_TIMESTAMP (1) so isOperation returns true (>0), but M's isOperation returns false (1==0 is false), causing a subsequent cancel call to revert in P (because isOperationPending fails) but succeed in M (incorrectly).

After scheduling an operation with delay 1 second and warping to make it ready, calling cancel with a proposer succeeds on P but reverts on M because M's isOperation returns false for the id due to the != 0 check returning false when timestamp equals _DONE_TIMESTAMP (1).

After scheduling an operation with delay 0 and executing it, calling cancel on the same id returns false (revert) due to isOperation returning false for _DONE_TIMESTAMP (1) in the buggy version, while it returns true in the reference because > 0 still returns true for 1.

After scheduling an operation with delay 1, warping to make it ready, then executing it, the reference's isOperation(id) returns true (since timestamp == _DONE_TIMESTAMP == 1 > 0), but the buggy version returns false (since 1 != 0), causing cancel(id) to succeed (returning true from try/catch) on the reference and revert on the buggy version.

After scheduling and executing an operation, cancel reverts on the buggy (M) because isOperation returns false for timestamp == 1, but succeeds on the reference (P) because isOperation returns true for timestamp > 0.

After scheduling an operation with delay 0 and executing it, calling cancel on the same id reverts in M (isOperation returns false because timestamp == 1 != 0) but succeeds in P (isOperation returns true because timestamp == 1 > 0).

Calling cancel with an operation ID whose timestamp is 0 should revert in the reference (since isOperation returns false) but succeed in the bug (since isOperation returns true due to 0 < 0 being false).

Calling cancel with an operation ID whose timestamp is 1 (the DONE timestamp) reverts in the reference (isOperationPending returns false) but succeeds in the buggy version (isOperationPending returns true because 1 < 0 is false).
